pos: n. (a son of Shamer, of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Yechubbah, hidden, or he will be hidden, from chava, to hide or conceal; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:34.
biblical_def: Jehubbah is a son of Shamer in the register of Asher: “And the sons of Shamer; Ahi, and Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram” (1 Chronicles 7:34). The chapter gives Asher a short genealogy and then a striking summary: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Asher is the tribe of which Jacob said that his bread should be fat and he should yield royal dainties, and of which Moses said he should dip his foot in oil. It produced no judge, no king and no prophet of record, and it is scarcely mentioned in the narrative books. Yet the Chronicler counts twenty-six thousand fighting men in it and calls its household heads choice and mighty. His name means hidden, and the tribe he belonged to is largely hidden in Scripture, and both are nevertheless numbered.

corruption_summary: A tribe with no famous son is assumed to have contributed nothing; the Chronicler counts twenty-six thousand men of valour in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Significance is measured by prominence, and by that measure Asher is negligible: no judge, no king, no prophet, barely a story. The Chronicler measures differently. He records the households, names the heads, and reports the muster, and the adjectives he uses — choice, mighty men of valour, chief of the princes — are the same he uses of Judah and Benjamin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's reckoning of a people is not the chronicler's reckoning of famous men. Moses blessed this tribe, “Let Asher be blessed with children; let him be acceptable to his brethren, and let him dip his foot in oil” (Deuteronomy 33:24). A son named hidden, in a tribe mostly hidden, under a blessing plainly given.

pos: n. (a son of Shamer, of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Rohgah, outcry, or clamour, of uncertain root; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:34.
biblical_def: Rohgah stands beside Jehubbah in the same clause: “And the sons of Shamer; Ahi, and Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram” (1 Chronicles 7:34). Four brothers, one verse, nothing more. The genealogy of Asher in this chapter is one of the shortest tribal records in Chronicles, and it is also one of the most emphatically commended: these men were “heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes” (1 Chronicles 7:40). The next verses list the sons of Helem and the sons of Japhlet, and then the tribe disappears from the book. Chronicles was written for a people who had lost almost everything and needed to know who they were. For a family of Asher, this verse was the whole of their standing in Israel, and it was enough to establish it.

corruption_summary: Records of ordinary families are read as filler; for the returned exiles they were the documentary proof of belonging to Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: The reader who skips 1 Chronicles 1 to 9 is skipping the foundation the rest of the book stands on. “So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, who were carried away to Babylon for their transgression” (1 Chronicles 9:1). The registers survived the deportation, and the Chronicler put them at the front because a people who could not prove their descent could not claim their land or their altar.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that belonging to the people of God is a definite thing, with boundaries and evidence, not an attitude a man adopts. Rohgah's name is in the Bible because his family needed it to be.

pos: n. (a priestly ancestor of Maasiai, among those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity)
etymology: Hebrew Yachzerah, may he lead back, or protection, of uncertain root; named once, 1 Chronicles 9:12.
biblical_def: Jahzerah appears inside a priestly pedigree: “And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer” (1 Chronicles 9:12). Chapter 9 lists those who came back from Babylon and settled in Jerusalem, and it is careful about the priests, giving each his full descent for several generations. The reason follows immediately: “And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God” (1 Chronicles 9:13). Seventeen hundred and sixty priests in one city, each of whom had to be able to show his line back to Aaron. Jahzerah is one link in one such chain, and without him the chain does not reach. The whole chapter is a demonstration that the God who sent Israel into captivity for her transgression also kept the records by which her worship could begin again.

corruption_summary: A line of names is treated as padding; for the post-exilic priesthood it was the legal warrant to approach the altar at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Long pedigrees invite skimming. But under the law, a priest who could not demonstrate his descent from Aaron was barred from the altar, and the returned community enforced it. The chain in 1 Chronicles 9:12 runs Maasiai, Adiel, Jahzerah, Meshullam, Meshillemith, Immer — six names to establish one man's right to minister.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that access to God has always been on terms God sets, and never on terms the worshipper assumes. The old warrant was ancestry, carefully kept; the new is better and surer, for our great high priest is “made, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life” (Hebrews 7:16). Jahzerah's place in a list is a small reminder of how seriously the first arrangement was taken.

pos: n. (the father of Zanoah, a son of Mered by Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh)
etymology: Hebrew Yequthi'el, the fear of God, or preservation of God, from a root signifying to preserve or to hope, with El, God; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:18.
biblical_def: Jekuthiel comes out of one of the strangest verses in the genealogies: “And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took” (1 Chronicles 4:18). An Egyptian princess married into the tribe of Judah, and her sons founded three towns of Judah — Gedor, Socho and Zanoah. The name Bithiah itself means daughter of the LORD, which is not a name an Egyptian king gave his child; it is the name she took, or was given, when she came into Israel. The verses around this one are full of craftsmen and townsmen: “These were the potters, and those that dwelt among plants and hedges: there they dwelt with the king for his work” (1 Chronicles 4:23). Jekuthiel's name means the fear of God, and his mother was a convert out of the house that had enslaved his father's people.

corruption_summary: Conversion is reframed as cultural exchange; Scripture calls Pharaoh's daughter by a Hebrew name meaning daughter of the LORD and counts her sons in Judah.
corruption_paragraphs: A modern reading of a marriage across nations reaches for blending and mutual enrichment. The text reaches for something sharper. Bithiah is not described as bringing Egypt into Judah; she is given a name that confesses the God of Israel, her sons are reckoned to Judah, and the towns they founded are Judah's towns. The movement is one-directional, and it is the direction of conversion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the covenant takes in the stranger on the covenant's terms, not on the stranger's. Ruth said it best: “thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (Ruth 1:16). An Egyptian princess made that exchange, and her son's name was the fear of God.

pos: n. (a name in the ancient record of the sons of Shelah, Judah's son)
etymology: Hebrew Yashuvi Lachem, he returned to Lehem, or bread-returner; the Authorized Version reads it as one name; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:22.
biblical_def: Jashubilehem closes one of the most remarkable verses in Chronicles: “And Jokim, and the men of Chozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who had the dominion in Moab, and Jashubilehem. And these are ancient things” (1 Chronicles 4:22). That last clause is the Chronicler's own note on his source: he is copying something very old, older than the material around it, and he says so rather than smoothing it into the rest. The record concerns the sons of Shelah, the third son of Judah, and the verse after it identifies their trade and their service: “These were the potters, and those that dwelt among plants and hedges: there they dwelt with the king for his work” (1 Chronicles 4:23). Potters and gardeners in the king's employ, with a tradition of dominion in Moab behind them, preserved in a document the Chronicler could date only as ancient. Scripture is content to hand on what it received without inventing the explanation it did not have.

corruption_summary: An obscure source is treated as grounds for suspecting the text; the Chronicler marks his own material as ancient and hands it on unaltered.
corruption_paragraphs: Where a passage is hard, the critical habit is to emend it, reassign it, or explain it away as a corrupted fragment. The Chronicler faced the same difficulty and took the opposite course: he copied what he had and wrote beside it, these are ancient things. He did not improve the record to make it legible, and the Holy Ghost preserved it in that state.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverence for the text as given, including the parts of it we cannot fully construe. “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever” (Deuteronomy 29:29). A difficult verse is not an invitation to rewrite Scripture; it is an occasion for humility before it.

pos: n. (the eleventh of the Gadite captains who came to David in the hold)
etymology: Hebrew Makbannay, clad with a mantle, or bond of the LORD, of uncertain root; named once, 1 Chronicles 12:13.
biblical_def: Machbanai is the last named of eleven Gadite captains who crossed over to David while he was an outlaw: “Jeremiah the tenth, Machbanai the eleventh” (1 Chronicles 12:13). The description of the company is one of the most vivid in Chronicles: “And of the Gadites there separated themselves unto David into the hold to the wilderness men of might, and men of war fit for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces were like the faces of lions, and were as swift as the roes upon the mountains” (1 Chronicles 12:8). Their rank is then given: “These were of the sons of Gad, captains of the host: one of the least was over an hundred, and the greatest over a thousand” (1 Chronicles 12:14). And how they came: “These are they that went over Jordan in the first month, when it had overflown all his banks” (1 Chronicles 12:15). They swam a flooded river in spring to join a man with no throne, no army and a king hunting him. Machbanai's name is eleventh on that list.

corruption_summary: Allegiance is given to the side already winning; eleven captains swam a flooded Jordan to join a fugitive with no kingdom.
corruption_paragraphs: Political loyalty ordinarily follows power, and the men of 1 Chronicles 12 had every reason to stay where they were. David was in a hold in the wilderness, under sentence from the reigning king, with a few hundred men in debt and distress. The Gadites came anyway, across a river in flood, and the Chronicler describes them in the language of lions and roes because what they did was extraordinary.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith commits itself to the anointed king before his kingdom is visible. That is precisely the shape of Christian allegiance now: “But now we see not yet all things put under him” (Hebrews 2:8). The Gadites were right about David before anyone could prove it, and their names are in Scripture for it.

pos: n. (the fourth of the Gadite captains who came to David in the hold)
etymology: Hebrew Mishmannah, fatness, or vigour, from shamen, to be fat or stout; named once, 1 Chronicles 12:10.
biblical_def: Mishmannah is fourth in the same roll: “Mishmannah the fourth, Jeremiah the fifth” (1 Chronicles 12:10). The list runs Ezer, Obadiah, Eliab, Mishmannah, Jeremiah, Attai, Eliel, Johanan, Elzabad, Jeremiah, Machbanai — eleven men, each given a number and nothing else. Their collective description carries the weight: men of might, fit for the battle, able with shield and buckler, faces like lions, swift as the roes upon the mountains (1 Chronicles 12:8). The chapter as a whole explains how David's following grew from a band of fugitives into a kingdom, tribe by tribe, until “there was joy in Israel” (1 Chronicles 12:40). The name Mishmannah means fatness or vigour, a word Scripture uses of strength and abundance, and it suits a man who crossed a river in flood in the first month to stand with a hunted king.

corruption_summary: Strength is treated as an end in itself; these men put their strength at the disposal of God's anointed while it cost them everything to do so.
corruption_paragraphs: Vigour, courage and martial skill are admired in the abstract and then attached to whatever cause pays for them. Chronicles will not let the admiration float free. The Gadites' strength is described at length and then located precisely: they separated themselves unto David, into the hold, to the wilderness. The virtue is in the direction as much as in the power.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that natural gifts are stewardship, not merit, and that their worth is settled by whose service they enter. The chapter ends with the whole nation at Hebron, “for there was joy in Israel” (1 Chronicles 12:40) — the end to which eleven men's courage in a wilderness hold had been quietly tending.

pos: n. (a son of Micah, in the descent of Saul through Jonathan; written Tarea in the parallel list)
etymology: Hebrew Tachrea, of uncertain derivation, perhaps cunning or flight; named once in this spelling, 1 Chronicles 9:41, and as Tarea at 1 Chronicles 8:35.
biblical_def: Tahrea belongs to the house of Saul, four generations down: “And the sons of Micah were, Pithon, and Melech, and Tahrea, and Ahaz” (1 Chronicles 9:41). The verse before it gives the line: “And the son of Jonathan was Meribbaal: and Meribbaal begat Micah” (1 Chronicles 9:40). Meribbaal is the man the books of Samuel call Mephibosheth, lamed as a child when his nurse fled on the day Saul and Jonathan died at Gilboa, found years later by David and given a place at the king's table for Jonathan's sake. Micah was his son; Tahrea was Micah's. The Chronicler carries the line on for several generations more, long after the house had any political standing. The parallel register at 1 Chronicles 8:35 spells the name Tarea, one of the ordinary variations between the two copies. A crippled man's descendants were still being counted among the chief men of Benjamin generations later, because David had kept an oath.

corruption_summary: A broken house is expected to end quietly; Jonathan's lame son was given a king's table and his great-grandsons were still being numbered in Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: The ordinary fate of a deposed dynasty is extinction, and Mephibosheth had every reason to expect it: “And Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up, and fled” (2 Samuel 4:4). What came instead was David's word: “Fear not: for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake” (2 Samuel 9:7).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the durability of covenant love. David kept faith with a dead friend by sustaining a crippled heir, and four generations later the Chronicler is still writing that family's names into the register of Benjamin. Oaths made before God outlive the men who swear them.

pos: n. (a son of Shaharaim by Hodesh, a head of the fathers in Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Shakhyah, fame of the LORD, or the LORD hath hedged about, of uncertain root; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:10.
biblical_def: Shachia is one of the sons born to Shaharaim in Moab: “And Jeuz, and Shachia, and Mirma. These were his sons, heads of the fathers” (1 Chronicles 8:10). The context is given a verse earlier: “And he begat of Hodesh his wife, Jobab, and Zibia, and Mesha, and Malcham” (1 Chronicles 8:9). Shaharaim had put away two wives and gone into the country of Moab, and there fathered a second family whose sons became heads of fathers' houses in Benjamin. The chapter's verdict on the whole company is plain: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). A household begun in exile from the tribal land ended up seated in the holy city, ruling fathers' houses. The Chronicler reports the domestic disorder without comment and reports the outcome without sentiment, which is his usual manner.

corruption_summary: A disordered household is assumed to forfeit its future; the sons born in Moab to a man who had put away his wives became chief men in Jerusalem.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture records Shaharaim's domestic history plainly: he “begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away” (1 Chronicles 8:8). No approval is expressed and no excuse offered. The Chronicler simply continues, and the sons of that second household are named as heads of fathers' houses who dwelt at Jerusalem.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's providence works through histories He does not approve, without thereby approving them. The honest record of a man's failures and the honest record of what God did afterward stand side by side in one chapter, and neither cancels the other.

etymology: Hebrew Mirmah, deceit, or fraud, from ramah, to beguile or deal treacherously; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:10.
biblical_def: Mirma is named last in his father's second family: “And Jeuz, and Shachia, and Mirma. These were his sons, heads of the fathers” (1 Chronicles 8:10). The name itself is a hard one. Mirmah in Hebrew is the ordinary word for deceit — the same word the psalmist sets against the blessed man, “Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile” (Psalm 32:2). Why a father gave a son such a name Scripture does not say, and the Chronicler makes nothing of it: the man is reckoned a head of the fathers like his brothers, among those who “dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Israel's names were not always flattering, and the Holy Ghost did not edit the register to improve them. A man called deceit sat as a chief in the holy city.

corruption_summary: Unflattering details are smoothed out of sacred records; the Hebrew registers kept a man called deceit and said nothing to soften it.
corruption_paragraphs: Every institution tidies its archive. Scripture does not. Among the heads of the fathers in Benjamin stands a man whose name is the Hebrew word for fraud, and no explanation, apology or allegory is supplied. The same book names Jabez whose mother bare him with sorrow, Benoni the son of my sorrow, and Ichabod, the glory is departed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honesty of the inspired record, which is one of the strongest arguments for its truthfulness. “Deceit is in the heart of them that imagine evil: but to the counsellors of peace is joy” (Proverbs 12:20). A forger improving a genealogy would not have left Mirma in it.
